items.a_text: Non-users and low users (1 hour per day) of screens generally do not differ in psychological well-being.
items.b_text: Light users of digital media exhibit slightly higher psychological well-being than non-users.
items.explanation: Claim A asserts that there is no difference in psychological well-being between non-users and low users, whereas Claim B asserts that light users have higher psychological well-being than non-users.

items.a_text: Rates of major depression increased in cohorts born after World War II.
items.b_text: Depression rates in children born between 1965 and 1996 showed no effect of year of birth.
items.explanation: Claim A asserts that depression rates increased in post-World War II birth cohorts, whereas Claim B finds no birth-year effect on depression rates for cohorts born between 1965 and 1996.

items.a_text: Results regarding the association between cyberbullying and self-harm or suicidality are conflicting.
items.b_text: Suicidal ideation is among the strongest associations with cyberbullying victimization.
items.explanation: Claim A states that evidence regarding the link between cyberbullying and suicidality is conflicting, whereas Claim B asserts a clear and strong association between cyberbullying victimization and suicidal ideation.

items.a_text: The decrease in adolescent psychological well-being may be at least partially due to the rapid adoption of smartphones and the subsequent shift in time use.
items.b_text: The estimated associations between daily digital technology usage and adolescents' well-being are unlikely to be of clinical or practical significance.
items.explanation: Claim A suggests that smartphone adoption meaningfully contributes to a decline in adolescent well-being, whereas Claim B asserts that the link between digital technology use and well-being is too small to be practically significant.

items.a_text: Facebook use over a two-week period predicts declines in overall life satisfaction over time.
items.b_text: The median longitudinal within-person effect of social media use on life satisfaction was trivial in size (beta = -0.05).
items.explanation: Claim A asserts that social media use predicts declines in life satisfaction over time, whereas Claim B finds that the longitudinal within-person effect of social media use on life satisfaction is trivial in size.

items.a_text: Cohort changes in depression rates cannot be fully attributed to artifacts of reporting, recall, mortality, or labeling.
items.b_text: There is no evidence for an increased prevalence of child or adolescent depression over the past 30 years when concurrent assessment is used.
items.explanation: Claim A asserts that historical changes in depression rates reflect real cohort shifts rather than measurement artifacts, whereas Claim B finds no evidence of increased depression prevalence when controlling for recall artifacts through concurrent assessment.
